Name: South-View founded
Body: In the decades following the Civil War, African Americans in Atlanta built vibrant, self-reliant communities, yet faced constant disrespect—even in death. Under Jim Crow practices, city cemeteries remained strictly segregated. At Oakland Cemetery, Black citizens were initially restricted to "Slave Square." Even after emancipation permitted plot purchases, mistreatment persisted. In 1877, city officials ordered the removal of bodies from Slave Square to make room for white burials, unceremoniously moving marked graves to pauper sections and burying others in mass graves. Years later, at Westview Cemetery, Black families were directed through a back gate to a segregated section named Rest Haven, where "the carriages had driven past the imposing stone gatehouse of Westview Cemetery and through a modest iron gate that stood several hundred yards beyond the main entrance" (Henderson 1). Despite expectations, Rest Haven suffered from severe neglect, as "the lack of maintenance for Westview's African American burials conflicts with the original intention of equal treatment that had been specified in 1884" (Henderson 11). Determined to provide dignity and honor to their loved ones, Albert Watts—whose own family had experienced this indignity—joined forces with five fellow Black businessmen and leaders: Jacob McKinley, George W. Graham, Rev. Robert Grant, Charles H. Morgan, and Rev. John Render. Together, they petitioned the city council in February 1886 to create a place for "dignified Christian burials" open to all people regardless of race (Henderson 13). Chartered in April 1886, South View was established not only out of necessity but also as a community endeavor and business enterprise. "From its inception, the cemetery operated as a stockholder corporation, making it one of the oldest African American–owned corporate enterprises in the United States" (Greenmellen). Since its creation, South-View has expanded from its original 25 acres to more than 100 acres and continues to serve the community as an active cemetery (Greenmellen).
Source:
1.  Henderson, D. L. South-View: An African American City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
2.  Greenmellen. “South-View Cemetery.” Georgia Historical Society, Georgia Historical Society, 22 May 2026, www.georgiahistory.com/ghmi_marker_updated/south-view-cemetery/.
3.  Bond, Ann Hill. “From Enslavement to Legacy: The History Buried at South-View Cemetery.” Atlanta, 6 Feb. 2026, atlanta.capitalbnews.org/south-view-cemetery-black-atlanta-history/.

Name: Reconstruction Era
Body:
When the Civil War ended in 1865, more than 460,000 newly freed people lived in Georgia. Reconstruction, which lasted until 1871 in Georgia and until 1877 elsewhere in the South, was the struggle over what their freedom would mean (Bragg).

For a few years, change came quickly. Freed people sought out schools and built all-Black churches. In Atlanta, 37 Black delegates helped write the state constitution of 1868, which provided for Black voting and free public schools. That year, 32 Black Republicans won seats in the Georgia legislature, including Henry McNeal Turner. White legislators expelled them in September 1868, and they were not reinstated until 1870. The Ku Klux Klan targeted Black leaders, and white conservative Democrats held full control of the state by January 1872 (Bragg; Angell).

South-View's founders lived through these years. Jacob McKinley built his businesses during Reconstruction, George W. Graham became one of the first two African Americans elected to the Atlanta City Council in 1871, and Robert Grant co-founded Zion Hill Baptist Church in 1872 (Henderson 18–21). In 1877, Atlanta's city council ordered the remains of those buried in Oakland Cemetery's "Slave Square" moved (Henderson). Nine years later, formerly enslaved African Americans founded South-View ("South-View Cemetery").
Source:
1.  Bragg, William Harris. “Reconstruction in Georgia.” *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 30 Sept. 2020, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/reconstruction-in-georgia/.
2.  Angell, Stephen Ward. “Henry McNeal Turner (1834–1915).” *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 14 Aug. 2020, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/henry-mcneal-turner-1834-1915/.
3.  Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
4.  Greenmellen. “South-View Cemetery.” Georgia Historical Society, Georgia Historical Society, 22 May 2026, www.georgiahistory.com/ghmi_marker_updated/south-view-cemetery/.

Name: Panic of 1893
Body: The Panic of 1893 unleashed a severe economic crisis across the United States. Striking an economy that had reached high output per person, the downturn triggered widespread panic as gold reserves dropped, leading depositors to convert bank notes to gold (Whitten; Pamela). As loan defaults rose and hundreds of banks failed, the crisis resulted in an estimated 14,000 business insolvencies and an unemployment rate exceeding ten percent for five to six consecutive years—a prolonged disaster matched only by the Great Depression (Whitten; Pamela). For the founders and officials of South-View Cemetery, navigating this financial devastation was a monumental undertaking. On August 7, 1893, Nicodemus Holmes and the board of directors petitioned the Atlanta City Council for tax relief. They argued that because of South-View's modest size and its commitment to burying the city’s impoverished paupers, the cemetery should be exempted from its $100 annual license fee. Their appeal was flatly denied. Despite this setback, South-View persevered, interring two-thirds of Atlanta’s African American dead throughout the Panic. The cemetery’s survival owed much to the sheer determination of its founders—men of varying financial means who had endured the far greater adversity of slavery. By 1900, South-View was providing graves for pauper burials at $1.35 per person, compared to at least $2.00 for white pauper burials. When South-View officials increased their bid to $2.00 to seek equal compensation, city council members attempted to negotiate a lower price; however, "South-View officials refused and stood behind their original bid for equal compensation" (Henderson 45). Consequently, the city awarded the contract to Oak View Cemetery at $1.50 per body, while also contracting private undertakers like Lucius L. Lee (Henderson 45-46). Today, many pauper graves lie in overgrown, wooded areas or unmarked plots. As D.L. Henderson observes, "The racial disparities in the cost of burial—in this instance, carried out through the city's control over the necessities of burial—paralleled the oppressive and often demeaning conditions of African American life from the nineteenth to the early twentieth century in Atlanta" (46). Ultimately, South-View's mission of offering a dignified burial could only mitigate municipal bigotry while serving as a crucial sanctuary of respect.
Source:
1.  Henderson, D. L. South-View: An African American City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
2.  Whitten, David O. “The Depression of 1893.” *EH.Net Encyclopedia*, edited by Robert Whaples, 14 Aug. 2001, eh.net/encyclopedia/the-depression-of-1893/.
3.  Pamela. “History in the Margins.” History in the Margins, 4 Sept. 2026, www.historyinthemargins.com/2026/09/05/the-great-panic-of-1893/.
Picture credit: “The recent panic,” New York Stock Exchange, May 5, 1893. Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper. Library of Congress. Public domain.

Name: Pittsburgh Riot
Body: In the early morning hours of May 17, 1902, violence erupted in the Pittsburgh neighborhood of Atlanta. Samuel A. Kerlin, a white former police officer, was walking down McDaniel Street when he encountered Will Richardson, an African American store owner whom Kerlin had previously arrested and testified against, causing him to spend months on a chain gang (National Park Service). Richardson threatened Kerlin and fired several shotgun shots; although Kerlin escaped, he returned around 1:30 a.m. with fellow officers and armed civilians to arrest Richardson at his grocery store on the corner of McDaniel and Amy streets (National Park Service). Richardson and his companions barricaded themselves inside with a heavy arsenal. As Kerlin's force approached, Richardson's group opened fire, killing an officer and sparking a full siege involving Atlanta police and thousands of armed civilians who traded an estimated 3,000 rounds over several hours (Henderson 116–17; National Park Service). To force the men out, the block was set on fire. The violence quickly turned into a broader assault on Black residents: "The New York Times reported that three thousand people—at least two thousand of them armed—surrounded the burning block of buildings," while mob members hunted residents, including James Harrison, who was chased along railroad tracks and "shot hundreds of times as he tried to escape the mob" (Henderson 116–17). Richardson perished inside the burning store, and his body was almost entirely cremated in the fire (Henderson 116–17; National Park Service). Tensions remained high following the destruction: "After the burned body of the negro was found, an angry mob of white men seized it and started with it towards the city," until Chief Ball formed a police cordon at the city limits to intercept the crowd and transport the body by wagon (Hartzog). In total, nine people died during the riot, and state militia troops were deployed to patrol the Pittsburgh community to maintain order (Henderson 116–17; National Park Service).
Source:
1.  Henderson, D. L. South-View: An African American City of the Dead. Carrelspin Press, 2018.
2.  Hartzog, Henry S. “Negro’s Deadly Aim: Ends Earthly Career of Three Officers and a Citizen.” The Bamberg Herald, 22 May 1902.
3.  *Pittsburgh Historic District*. National Register of Historic Places Registration Form, National Park Service, https://npgallery.nps.gov/pdfhost/docs/NRHP/Text/06000503.pdf.

Name: 1906 Atlanta Massacre
Body:
At the turn of the twentieth century, Atlanta promoted itself as the gleaming hub of the "New South"—a vibrant city of economic progress and modern opportunity. Yet beneath this optimistic façade lay deep-seated racial segregation and prejudice. As the city's African American population expanded to tens of thousands, Black Atlantans built thriving businesses, churches, schools, and self-managed institutions like South-View Cemetery. However, this remarkable progress ignited resentment among some white residents, sparking fierce economic competition and racial friction across all levels of society.

By the summer of 1906, political strife reached a boiling point during a contentious gubernatorial campaign. Sensationalized newspaper headlines falsely accused Black men of attacking white women, stoking fears and racial animosity throughout the city. On the evening of September 22, tensions exploded as a mob of nearly ten thousand white men and boys flooded downtown Atlanta. For hours, violence consumed streets like Decatur, Pryor, and Peachtree. Black-owned businesses were looted and vandalized, streetcars were raided, and innocent residents—including young messenger Frank Smith—were brutally attacked and killed.

As night fell, heavy rains helped disperse the downtown mobs, but the terror spread toward Black neighborhoods like Brownsville. Defending their homes and families, local residents organized resistance. When police officers and armed civilians invaded Brownsville on September 24, a deadly skirmish ensued. State militia moved in, disarming the community and arresting hundreds of Black residents, including educators and leaders like Dr. J.W.E. Bowen and Luther Judson Price, while Civil War veteran George Union Wilder was murdered in the unrest.

When the violence finally subsided, dozens of Black citizens lay dead and countless others were wounded or displaced. The massacre shattered Atlanta's progressive image on the national stage. In response, local Black and white leaders formed interracial committees to restore peace, yet systemic disenfranchisement soon followed through restrictive voting laws in 1908. Despite these crushing setbacks, community institutions like South-View Cemetery endured—serving as both a final resting place for victims and heroes, and an enduring monument to resilience, memory, and the ongoing pursuit of justice.
Source: 1. Bauerlein, Mark. *Negrophobia: A Race Riot in Atlanta, 1906*. Encounter Books, 2001.  2. “Stories from the Soil.” *Fulton County Remembrance Coalition*, https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil.  3. South-View Cemetery Association. *In Remembrance of The 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre*. Brochure.
Picture credit: The Atlanta Constitution, front page, September 23, 1906. Public domain (via Wikimedia Commons).

Name: Civil Rights Movement
Body:
The struggle for civil rights is not a self-contained chapter in history, but a continuous story that connects the era of Reconstruction through the 1960s to the present day. To understand this movement fully, we must look beyond the most celebrated figures and examine both nationwide efforts and the deeply rooted local activism in cities like Atlanta.

While leaders such as Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, Rosa Parks, Thurgood Marshall, and John Lewis helped shape the public consciousness, countless less heralded figures—including Ralph David Abernathy Sr., Joseph Lowery, Herman Russell, C.T. Vivian, Hosea Williams, Andrew Young Jr., Julian Bond, Joseph E. Boone, Lonnie C. King Jr., and Dr. Roslyn Pope—fought tirelessly against everyday indignities. Organisations like the Black Panther Party, alongside initiatives like the South-View & Praise House project, underscore how everyday stories and local spaces were crucial to sustaining the wider movement.

From the Montgomery Bus Boycotts and sit-ins to pivotal marches across historic locations like the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma and the March on Washington, these events transformed the nation. By honoring both the major milestones and the smaller, overlooked personal stories, we preserve a richer, more accurate history of the ongoing fight for equality.
Source: Team notes.

Name: Atlanta Child Murders
Body:
In the late 1970s, a quiet anxiety began to shadow Atlanta’s low-income Black neighborhoods as crime rates climbed with little national notice. Between 1979 and 1981, that shadow deepened into a terrifying crisis when nearly thirty young African American children, teenagers, and young adults went missing. The horror began in late July 1979 with the disappearances of 14-year-old Edward Hope Smith and 13-year-old Alphred James Evans, both found dead shortly after. Over the next twenty-two months, young residents vanished in plain daylight from public places, their bodies later discovered in isolated areas. The fear grew unbearable as more children—14-year-old Milton Harvey and 9-year-old Yusef Bell—were lost to the darkness. As noted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, during this period "at least 28 African-American children, teenagers, and young adults... were killed in the Atlanta area" ("Serial Killers, Part 5"). Desperate for answers, grieving parents and grassroots community leaders banded together on April 15, 1980, forming the Committee to Stop Children’s Murders (STOP) to run hotlines, raise public awareness, and press law enforcement into recognizing a pattern ("Atlanta Child Murders"). While local police initially treated each case independently, the overwhelming crisis eventually compelled the Atlanta Police Department to establish the Missing and Murdered Task Force in August 1980 ("Atlanta Child Murders").

Federal help arrived after the June 1980 abduction of a 7-year-old girl prompted local officials to request broader support. Special Agent in Charge John Glover—the first African American to lead an FBI field office—pledged full institutional backing, bringing over two dozen full-time agents into a major federal inquiry by late autumn ("Serial Killers, Part 5"). As investigators pieced together the clues, they realized a single perpetrator was likely targeting young Black males. By spring 1981, when the killer began discarding victims in the Chattahoochee River, law enforcement set up tense, round-the-clock stakeouts across fourteen metro river bridges ("Serial Killers, Part 5"). The turning point came at 2:52 a.m. on May 22, 1981, when officers stationed near a bridge heard a loud splash and spotted a car speeding away ("Serial Killers, Part 5"). They pulled over 23-year-old Wayne Williams. Though initially let go, the recovery of Nathaniel Cater’s body downstream two days later centered the investigation squarely on Williams ("Serial Killers, Part 5"). With circumstantial evidence mounting—including hair and fiber matches, a lack of an alibi, and failed polygraph tests—authorities arrested Williams on June 21, 1981 ("Atlanta Child Murders"). As documented on the Atlanta Child Murders memorial site, "Williams was convicted of the murders of two adults... and the police attributed most of the remaining child murders to him as well" (Atlanta’s Missing & Murdered). Though he was sentenced to consecutive life terms, bringing a close to the official investigation, the profound pain and systemic inequalities exposed during those tragic years left an indelible mark on the city of Atlanta.

Williams was convicted in 1982 of the murders of two adults. He has never been convicted in any of the children’s deaths, and he has always maintained his innocence. In 2019, Atlanta officials announced that evidence from the murders would be re-tested ("Atlanta Child Murders Case Reopened").
Source:
1.  “Serial Killers, Part 5: Wayne Williams and the Atlanta Child Murders.” FBI, FBI, 7 Feb. 2014, www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders.
2.  “Atlanta Child Murders: Law: Research Starters: Ebscohost.” EBSCO, www.ebsco.com/research-starters/law/atlanta-child-murders/. Accessed 27 Oct. 2026.
3.  Atlanta’s Missing & Murdered, atkid.weebly.com/. Accessed 27 Oct. 2026.
4.  “Atlanta Child Murders Case Reopened Months Before ‘Mindhunter.’” *Rolling Stone*, https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/culture-news/atlanta-child-murders-case-reopened-mindhunter-874051/. Accessed 1 Nov. 2026.
5.  “Atlanta Child Murders: Who Were the Victims?” *The Atlanta Journal-Constitution*, https://www.ajc.com/news/crime--law/atlanta-child-murders-who-were-the-victims/JzKvG4Yd4i2l0QGiURZ5XI/. Accessed 1 Nov. 2026.

Name: Jacob McKinley
Body: Jacob McKinley (1830–1896) was born into slavery in Newnan, Georgia, around 1830. Showing early promise and dedication, he began training as a carpenter at age 16—a craft he mastered so well that by 1853 he was sold for $1,550. When freedom arrived with the end of the Civil War, McKinley seized every opportunity to build his own destiny. Throughout Reconstruction, he established and acquired a diverse array of enterprises, eventually employing up to 150 Black and white workers. As historical records note, "He became a prosperous merchant, real estate owner, and a dealer in wood and coal; he owned a brickyard, a grocery store and a large amount of real estate" (pg. 18). When he joined his fellow visionaries to found South-View Cemetery, his real estate and personal holdings totaled $6,800 (equivalent to between $242,326 and $243,744 today), making him the wealthiest of the group. Unlike most of his co-founders, McKinley's final resting place is in his family's private plot at Oakland Cemetery.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 18.  2. “South-View Cemetery: The Oldest African American Controlled Burial Ground in Atlanta, Georgia.” *Building Memories*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/southview-cemetery/.

Name: Charles H. Morgan
Body: Charles H. Morgan (?–1886), a South Carolina native whose birth date remains lost to history, moved to Atlanta after the Civil War to work as a carriage trimmer. His meticulous craftsmanship in fashioning intricate leatherwork earned him high acclaim and allowed him to accumulate the capital needed to chart his own path. By 1881, Morgan had launched a thriving grocery store on Wheat Street. Beyond his commercial endeavors, he was a pillar of civic and spiritual life, helping establish the First Congregational Church and serving as a trustee for Atlanta University. In 1883, his daughter Rebecca—his only child with wife Anna—married tailor shop owner John C. "Jack" Huggins. The milestone was celebrated in the Atlanta Constitution as a highlight of "high colored life," describing a church sanctuary "literally packed with white and colored people" (pg. 18). In 1886, Morgan made history by purchasing the first three shares in South-View Cemetery; tragically, he passed away just three days later and was buried on December 17, 1886.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 18.  2. “South-View Cemetery: The Oldest African American Controlled Burial Ground in Atlanta, Georgia.” *Building Memories*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/southview-cemetery/.
Picture credit: Charles H. Morgan. Photo courtesy of the South-View Cemetery Association (via Georgia Tech's Building Memories).

Name: George W. Graham
Body: George W. Graham (1833–1894), born in Georgia, also began his journey as an enslaved carpenter. Though deprived of a formal education, Graham harbored ambitious political aspirations. In 1871, he shattered barriers by becoming one of the first two African Americans elected to the Atlanta City Council, representing the predominantly Black Third Ward. His victory sparked fierce backlash, with the Atlanta Daily Sun mocking his literacy and branding him "a negro without the business qualifications" for office (pg. 19). Undeterred, Graham served on the Printing and the Wells, Pumps, and Cisterns committees, successfully securing vital water lines for Martin and Richmond streets. He later worked in railroad shops, ran a drayage business, and opened a prosperous grocery store. By 1880, the Georgia Tax Digest valued his property at $1,490, and the Weekly Constitution recognized him as one of the city's leading African American property owners (pg. 20). By 1890, his net worth reached nearly $3,000, including $525 in South-View shares. Upon his death on September 5, 1894, the Atlanta Constitution honored him as a "pioneer of the colored people ... one of the oldest and most respected colored men of Atlanta" (pg. 19).
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 19–20.  2. “South-View Cemetery: The Oldest African American Controlled Burial Ground in Atlanta, Georgia.” *Building Memories*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/southview-cemetery/.

Name: John Render
Body: John Render (1845–1923) was born in Meriwether County, Georgia, to Daniel and Anne Render. A drayman by trade and a minister at heart, he married Laura Herenton of South Carolina, though they had no children. In 1886, Render invested in two shares of South-View Cemetery while simultaneously helping charter the Georgia Real Estate Loan and Trust Company. His deep community involvement extended to politics—running for Second Ward city councilman in 1890—and to faith leadership, serving as treasurer of the African Methodist Episcopal Church Ministers Union. He was also a staunch supporter and trustee of Morris Brown College (pg. 20). Render passed away in 1923 and was laid to rest at South-View, where his wife Laura joined him in 1945.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 20.  2. “South-View Cemetery: The Oldest African American Controlled Burial Ground in Atlanta, Georgia.” *Building Memories*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/southview-cemetery/.

Name: Robert Grant
Body: Robert Grant (1826–1896) was born in Washington, Wilkes County, Georgia. Largely self-taught, he learned his alphabet with help from local boys and entered a blacksmith apprenticeship at age 14, working at the anvil for twelve years. While still enslaved, he began preaching on his master's front porch. By 1869, Grant was ordained and earning his living as a drayman. He married his wife Eveline by 1870, raising two children. In 1872, he co-founded Zion Hill Baptist Church, initially holding services under a brush arbor while raising funds for a building on Humphries Street. The congregation grew to over 400 members, with property valued at $700 and Grant receiving an annual salary of $400 (for context, Big Bethel AME Church was valued at $18,000 and its pastor earned $1,200) (pg. 21). Two years later, Grant invested two-thirds of his annual earnings into three shares of South-View. Illness eventually forced him from the pulpit, and upon his death in 1896, he was laid to rest at South-View.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 21.  2. “Pastor Grant.” *Zion Hill Baptist Church*, https://www.zionhill.org/history/grant.

Name: Albert Watts
Body: Albert Watts (c. 1843–1903), a Clarke County native, was recorded as a 27-year-old laborer at the Glenn & Wright freight house on a 1870 bank application. Raised in a large family alongside parents Sterling and Emily, four siblings, and four half-siblings, Watts lived on Luckie Street before opening his own Fraser Street grocery store by 1874. In 1886, he co-founded South-View Cemetery and became its founding treasurer, serving until his death. Active in local politics, he championed temperance and chaired the Third Ward Colored Prohibition Club. He married Sarah Andrews and raised six surviving children of nine. By his death in 1903, his cemetery stock reached $200. Watts sparked a multigenerational legacy: his son Lewis Gould Watts served as secretary until 1936; grandson Albert Hawes Watts served as secretary, treasurer, president, and became the first African American on the American Cemetery Association board; and great-granddaughter Winifred Watts Hemphill was elected president of the South-View Cemetery Association in 2003. Albert, Lewis, and Albert Hawes all rest together in the family lot at South-View (pg. 22).
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 22.  2. “South-View Cemetery: The Oldest African American Controlled Burial Ground in Atlanta, Georgia.” *Building Memories*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/southview-cemetery/.
Picture credit: Albert Watts. Photo courtesy of the South-View Cemetery Association (via Georgia Tech's Building Memories).

Name: Nicodemus Holmes
Body: South-View's first president. A prosperous shoe store owner and one of the original stockholders of the cemetery. "...Nicodemus Holmes, who was both a secular and religious leader, apparently were attracted to the investment opportunity that South-View offered, as well as the appeal of acting in a leadership role within an African American enterprise" (p. 27). In 1893, he and the South-View board of directors signed a petition for tax relief submitted to the Atlanta City Council. While the petition was denied, he is credited as being one of the main figures who helped to guide South-View through the depression.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 27.

Name: Mitchell Cargile
Body: Mitchell Cargile was born in 1811 in Monticello, Georgia. In the mid-1850s, Cargile purchased his own time from his Monticello slaveholder and relocated to Atlanta where he worked as a carpenter. Enslaved people like Cargile, who had practical skills, such as carpentry or barbering, might be allowed to seek extra work and keep a portion of their earnings—income that could be used to purchase their freedom, if the slaveholder was willing. In Cargile's case, while freedom may not have been an option, he was able to pay the slaveholder to be allowed to live and work on his own. After emancipation, Cargile opened an undertaking business. By 1874, Cargile was advertising his skills as a "manufacturer of burial cases" in the Atlanta Constitution. He was listed in the 1876 Atlanta City Directory as a cabinet maker and undertaker. Cargile conducted business not only in Atlanta but throughout the South as well. He trained his sons in carpentry, and his son Lewis eventually joined him in the undertaking business. Cargile was a well-respected and prosperous businessman. In 1881, after he was implicated in a scheme to obtain a corpse for a medical college, he quickly responded by issuing a "Correction" to the Atlanta Constitution. Cargile wrote an explanation of the matter and insisted that he "had never yet violated a trust imposed by the friends of the dead, rich or poor." Cargile acquired a large amount of Atlanta real estate in the 1880s, and he was a board member and shareholder in the South-View Cemetery Association. In his later years, Cargile suffered financial setbacks, and in the Panic of 1893 he lost a hearse when he was forced to default on its mortgage. Cargile died in 1896 and was buried at South-View. His son Lewis continued to operate the family business.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 47–48.

Name: Lucius L. Lee
Body:
An undertaker who handled many of the earliest burials at South-View. He won the annual contract for pauper burials in 1904. For $1.40, Lee provided a shroud, made the coffin, and transported the body to the cemetery. "The same services for white American paupers buried at Westview cost the city $10 and included a 'factory-made coffin, lined and trimmed' for $6 or $7. The next year Lee raised his bid to $2.50 and lost the contract to David T. Howard who submitted a low bid of $1.24. This striking difference in the amount allocated to undertakers for the burial of white and African American paupers illustrates Atlanta's unequal treatment of impoverished African Americans in death."

Lucius Lee was born enslaved in Covington, Georgia, in 1854. He came to Atlanta after the Civil War, and at the age of fifteen he was working at O. H. Jones' livery stable. Later he learned the undertaking business while employed with a white American undertaker, Charles H. Swift. Lee owned and operated his own undertaking establishment on Decatur Street for almost thirty years. On the night of January 15, 1898, the Atlanta police called Lee to pick up a corpse at the corner of Mitchell and Whitehall Street. A man had collapsed and apparently died suddenly of a hemorrhage from the lungs. When Lee arrived with his wagon, he was shocked. He not only recognized the man, he also identified him as his wife's brother who was visiting from Macon. "I was struck speechless," said Lee. His brother-in-law had been at Lee's undertaking shop only an hour before. He had appeared to be in good health, despite having a history of lung problems. Lee's son William joined him in the business, and the establishment became "L. L. Lee & Son." Lucius Lee died in 1915 after an illness lasting more than a year. He was a member of several benevolent and fraternal orders, including the Masons, Odd Fellows, Knights of Pythias, and the Knights and Daughters of Tabor. His funeral was held at Big Bethel AME Church and was conducted according to the rites of the Knights and Daughters of Tabor. Lee's death occurred during the annual Tabor convention in Savannah, Georgia, and his funeral was delayed until the Tabor officials returned to Atlanta. Lee was buried in the lot he had purchased at South-View in 1886, next to his wife, Julia, who had died in 1912.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 46, 48–49.

Name: David T. Howard
Body: David Tobias Howard was born on December 10, 1849, in Knoxville, Georgia, on the plantation of Thomas C. Howard. After the Civil War and emancipation, David T. Howard learned to read and write while working in the railroad shop of R. C. Robson. Robson was a prominent railroad executive and brother-in-law of Thomas C. Howard. By working as a Pullman porter, David T. Howard accumulated more than $1,000 in taxable property. When R. C. Robson died in 1882, he bequeathed $200 to "Toby." This was likely a portion of the money Howard used to open an undertaking business in 1883. An 1890 advertisement for Howard's funeral home touted the first African American undertaker in Georgia to graduate from the Clarke School of Embalming (sometimes spelled "Clark"). The embalming school founded by Joseph Henry Clarke in Cincinnati, Ohio, was considered the leading institution in the field of funeral education, and it offered training for both white and African American undertakers. In 1887, Howard famously arranged for the burial of the "dynamite patient," James Terrell. Terrell had come to Atlanta seeking treatment for stomach cancer. A local doctor concocted a solution of small dynamite pellets dissolved in water. He administered the potion in drops to treat the skeletal Terrell, who was visibly wasting away. The treatment initially seemed to have some positive effect, but the patient succumbed to his illness a few days later. Terrell's race was not mentioned in the article, but Howard was engaged to bury his body in the pauper grounds at Westview. Throughout his fifty-year career, Howard's motto, "Treat Everyone Right," earned him a wide reputation for fairness and reliability. In the earlier years of his career, he was once challenged to uphold that business slogan. In March 1903, the Atlanta Dental College engaged Howard to arrange the burial of eighteen corpses that had been used for dissection by dental students. Howard hired two men to deliver the bodies to Oak View Cemetery, but when a lightning storm prevented them from reaching the cemetery, the drivers abandoned the wagon and left the corpses behind. The two drivers were arrested for their negligence in unlawfully disposing of the corpses, but when Howard later attempted to complete the delivery to Oak View, the cemetery refused to take the bodies. He reportedly regretted his decision to accept the contract and lamented the ongoing complications in settling the matter. The discarded bodies, both white and African American, were eventually interred at South-View. David T. Howard Jr. (d. 1912), a first honor graduate of the Clarke School of Embalming, joined his father in the business and took charge of the embalming for the funeral home. The younger Howard was honored as "one of the most proficient and capable embalmers in the United States" by his alma mater, and one of his embalmed specimens was placed on display in the school's museum in Cincinnati. His brothers Frank and Henry (d. 1945) and sisters Julia and Eleanor also worked in the family business. Howard senior opened a new funeral home at 71 Piedmont Avenue in 1930. The home was elaborately equipped and even featured a pipe organ, "the only one of its kind in use among colored funeral directors in the state of Georgia." In later years the business was known as David T. Howard & Company, and Eleanor Howard Murphy continued to manage the business after her father's death. She is buried at Oakland Cemetery in the Murphy family lot. David T. Howard's own funeral arrangements and interment at South-View in 1935 were handled by two of Atlanta's historic African American funeral homes, Ivey Brothers and Cox Brothers.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018.  2. “South-View Cemetery: The Oldest African American Controlled Burial Ground in Atlanta, Georgia.” *Building Memories*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/southview-cemetery/.
Picture credit: David T. Howard (in the carriage) with his mother and wife, about 1899. Library of Congress, African American Photographs Assembled for the 1900 Paris Exposition. Public domain.

Name: George Washington
Body: An indispensable element in caring for the dead in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries was the carriage, or hack, driver. George Washington (d. 1890) worked for Miller & Brady, one of Atlanta's oldest livery stables. In his twenty years of employment, Washington was said to have driven in more Atlanta funeral processions than anyone else in the city. He made frequent trips to Westview, Oakland, and South-View. Washington lived on Wheat Street, and his funeral service was held at Big Bethel AME church. The hearse and the funeral carriages were furnished free of charge by his employer and other liverymen. H. M. Patterson, a white American funeral director, provided Washington's casket, saying, "His funeral shan't cost his family one cent. We owe him that much for he was a faithful and honest servant."
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 50.

Name: Will Richardson
Body: Man accused of assaulting officer S. A. Kerlin. He was killed in the Riot of 1902.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 116–17.  2. *Pittsburgh Historic District*. National Register of Historic Places Registration Form, National Park Service, https://npgallery.nps.gov/pdfhost/docs/NRHP/Text/06000503.pdf.

Name: James Harrison
Body: Innocent bystander. A crowd of onlookers chased him when he was spotted walking along the railroad tracks during the Pittsburgh Riot, and he was shot as he tried to escape the mob.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, pp. 116–17.

Name: Milton Risdon
Body: One of Will Richardson's companions. He was wounded as he fled the burning buildings during the riot, then arrested and taken to jail. He was buried at South-View along with Richardson.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 116.

Name: George Union Wilder
Body: One of the officers reported that Wilder was "carrying a muzzle-loading musket when he was shot down" in Brownsville, a middle class neighborhood. He was the oldest African-American victim and had fought in the Civil War.
Source: 1. Bauerlein, Mark. *Negrophobia: A Race Riot in Atlanta, 1906*. Encounter Books, 2001, p. 198.  2. “Stories from the Soil.” *Fulton County Remembrance Coalition*, https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil.

Name: Frank Smith
Body: Telegraph office messenger.
Source: 1. “Stories from the Soil.” *Fulton County Remembrance Coalition*, https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil.

Name: John Wesley Edward Bowen Sr.
Body:
Born in New Orleans to a former enslaved carpenter who fought for the Union Army, John Wesley Edward Bowen Sr. served as President and Professor of Historical Theology at Gammon Theological Seminary.

Growing up during Reconstruction, Bowen possessed an insatiable thirst for knowledge. After completing his early studies, he taught classical languages before earning a Bachelor of Sacred Theology at Boston University—where his classmates chose him as commencement speaker—and becoming the university's first Black PhD graduate in 1887, as well as only the second African American in the nation to earn a doctorate.

Driven by a vision of racial equality within the church, Bowen served as a pastor and advocated tirelessly for Black bishops. His academic leadership brought him to Atlanta in 1893, where he became the first full-time Black professor at Gammon Theological Seminary. It was in Atlanta that he built a life with his wife Ariel, a music teacher at Clark College, and raised four children. In 1895, he commanded national attention at the Atlanta Cotton States Exposition with his stirring speech, "An Appeal to the King," challenging the nation to see the "Negro problem" as a universal human race problem.

By 1904, Bowen co-founded The Voice of the Negro, the South's first Black-edited literary journal, reaching over 15,000 subscribers. Yet personal and national tragedy soon tested his resolve. That same year, Ariel passed away. Two years later, as newly appointed president of Gammon, Bowen transformed the campus into a sanctuary for Black residents fleeing the horrors of the 1906 Atlanta Massacre. When he called the police for protection, officers instead severely beat and arrested him, sweeping him up among the 250 Black residents in Brownsville detained for possessing arms and under suspicion in the death of white policeman James Heard. Undeterred, Bowen dedicated nearly four decades of service to Gammon until his retirement in 1932, leaving a legacy carried on by his son, who became a Methodist bishop, before his death in 1933.
Source: 1. South-View Cemetery Association. *In Remembrance of The 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre*. Brochure.

Name: Alonzo Herndon
Body: Born into slavery, Alonzo Herndon persevered to build a prominent business empire, founding the Atlanta Life Insurance Company and opening three prominent barbershops, including the magnificent Crystal Palace at 66 Peachtree Street in 1902. When the racial violence of 1906 shook Atlanta, Herndon stood firm as his hard-won enterprises and community standing faced direct threats from the mob. That fateful Saturday night, rioters smashed the front windows of his Peachtree Street barbershop, and a violent mob ran down and murdered one of his workers, Fred Walton—a lame bootblack with a withered foot (The Herndons pp. 85–86).
Source: 1. Henderson, Alexa Benson. “Alonzo Herndon (1858–1927).” *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 20 Sept. 2004, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/business-economy/alonzo-herndon-1858-1927/.  2. Merritt, Carole. *The Herndons: An Atlanta Family*. University of Georgia Press, 2002, pp. 85–86.

Name: Luther Judson Price
Body: A businessman and postmaster in Brownsville, Price operated a general store that also housed the community's post office. During the massacre, white mobs accused him of supplying weapons and ammunition to Black residents defending their neighborhood. He was arrested and taken to the Fulton County jail, but the charges were eventually dropped.
Source: 1. *A Celebration of Life Honoring Albert Hawes Watts*. 26 Nov. 2001, *Digital Library of Georgia*, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/aarl_afpc_wattsalberthawes20011126.

Name: Marshall Carter
Body: A 13-year-old schoolboy who lived on Love Street near Summerhill. Carter was attacked during the first night of the massacre and suffered a fractured skull. He died at Grady Hospital on September 22, 1906. His identity as a victim of the massacre was confirmed in 2023 through historical death records.

Name: Stinson Ferguson
Body: A 25-year-old African American man who lived on Thurmond Street in northwest Atlanta. Ferguson was shot in the abdomen during the first night of violence and was pronounced dead upon arrival at Grady Hospital. Like Marshall Carter, his death was officially connected to the massacre through research completed in 2023.

Name: Henry Hugh Proctor
Body: As pastor of the First Congregational Church and a close associate of Booker T. Washington, Henry Hugh Proctor watched his congregation and city suffer through the devastation of 1906. In the aftermath of the riots, he worked tirelessly alongside other leaders to offer sanctuary, organize vital relief, and pave a path toward rebuilding peace, establishing both the Atlanta Civic League and the Colored Co-operative Civic League—which grew to mobilize over 1,500 members each in pursuit of community restoration.
Source: 1. Bevington, Paula Lawton. “Henry Hugh Proctor (1868–1933).” *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 13 Aug. 2013, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/henry-hugh-proctor-1868-1933/.

Name: John Wesley Dobbs
Body: Working as a 24-year-old railway clerk when the massacre erupted, John Wesley Dobbs was living on Auburn Avenue with his newlywed wife, Irene, in her sister's home. As violent mobs terrorized the city, Dobbs spent sleepless nights standing guard over the household with a revolver in hand—an ordeal that left him with a burning anger over the injustice that stayed with him for the rest of his life.
Source: 1. Bailey, Matthew. “John Wesley Dobbs (1882–1961).” *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 26 Aug. 2005, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/history-archaeology/john-wesley-dobbs-1882-1961/.

Name: Moses Amos
Body: As Georgia's first licensed African American pharmacist, Moses Amos built a pioneering career serving the Atlanta community. On September 22, 1906, as tensions boiled over near Five Points, police warned him to close his drugstore immediately because violent unrest was imminent and officers admitted they would be unable to protect him or his establishment (pg. 139).
Source: 1. South-View Cemetery Association. *In Remembrance of The 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre*. Brochure.  2. Bauerlein, Mark. *Negrophobia: A Race Riot in Atlanta, 1906*. Encounter Books, 2001, p. 139.

Name: Peter James Bryant
Body: Serving as pastor of the Wheat Street Baptist Church, Peter James Bryant was a guiding spiritual force during Atlanta's darkest hours. In the wake of the 1906 riots, he hosted Black religious leaders at his church to form the Christian Civic League, firmly believing that putting Christian principles into practice was essential to restoring positive racial relations across the community.
Source: 1. South-View Cemetery Association. *In Remembrance of The 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre*. Brochure.

Name: W. F. Penn
Body: A Yale graduate and prominent physician, Dr. W. F. Penn stood as one of Atlanta's most distinguished Black medical professionals. At a tense interracial Chamber of Commerce meeting on September 25, 1906, Penn passionately addressed white leaders, asking: “If living a sober, industrious, upright life … is not the standard by which a colored man can live and be protected in the South, what is to become of him? … Shall I leave and go North?”
Source: 1. South-View Cemetery Association. *In Remembrance of The 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre*. Brochure.

Name: David T. Howard
Body: A revered mortician and philanthropist who rose to become one of Atlanta’s first Black millionaires, David T. Howard faced the grim realities of the riot firsthand. When summoned to South Atlanta to retrieve the body of a Black riot victim, Howard made the startling discovery that the deceased man was actually white, but his face had been intentionally blackened with makeup or shoe polish (pp. 175–76).
Source: 1. Bauerlein, Mark. *Negrophobia: A Race Riot in Atlanta, 1906*. Encounter Books, 2001, pp. 175–76.

Name: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner
Body: An influential AME Bishop, former Georgia State Legislator, and outspoken activist, Bishop Henry McNeal Turner refused to counsel passive submission in the face of violence. As racial hostility escalated in 1906, Turner boldly advised Black citizens to buy firearms to defend themselves against "negrophobic whites" (pg. 34).
Source: 1. Angell, Stephen Ward. “Henry McNeal Turner (1834–1915).” *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 3 Sept. 2002, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/henry-mcneal-turner-1834-1915.  2. Bauerlein, Mark. *Negrophobia: A Race Riot in Atlanta, 1906*. Encounter Books, 2001, p. 34.

Name: William Crogman
Body: Serving as the first Black president of Clark College, William Crogman was a distinguished educator and community leader. In the terrifying wake of the riot, Crogman stepped forward as one of the key figures whose steadfast leadership and civic cooperation helped restore calm and preserve general stability in Atlanta (pg. 212).
Source: 1. South-View Cemetery Association. *In Remembrance of The 1906 Atlanta Race Massacre*. Brochure.  2. Bauerlein, Mark. *Negrophobia: A Race Riot in Atlanta, 1906*. Encounter Books, 2001, p. 212.

Name: Frank Smith
Body: A 19-year-old Western Union messenger who was attacked by a white mob on September 22, 1906. He was stabbed, struck with stones, and thrown from the Forsyth Street bridge in downtown Atlanta. He was buried at South-View Cemetery, where his gravestone still stands.
Source: 1. “Stories from the Soil.” *Fulton County Remembrance Coalition*, https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil.

Name: William Welch
Source: 1. “Stories from the Soil.” *Fulton County Remembrance Coalition*, https://www.fultonremembrance.org/remembrance-project/stories-from-the-soil.

Name: Samuel F. Ware
Body: He was the son of Lessie Lee and the nephew of Atlanta undertaker Lucius L. Lee. In 1916, he arrived in Atlanta, around the same time that his cousin and Lucius's son, Will Lee, had passed away, leaving the Lee undertaker business without any leadership. Not much was known about Samuel's life or business experience outside of the fact that he was a veteran of the Spanish-American War. On the night of Friday, December 8th, police apprehended two men caught digging up a casket from a fresh grave in South-View. Upon interrogation, the men claimed that Samuel Ware had hired them to recover the caskets allegedly for the purpose of reselling them. That same night, police found Samuel transporting two caskets that appeared to have been recently unearthed, followed by more discovered in his undertaking establishment. Samuel Ware and the two men were all arrested, with Ware's bail being set to $10,000. Samuel Ware was later replaced as president of the Atlanta Undertaking Company, with the stockholders disavowing any knowledge or involvement in his crimes. Ware was later convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison. However, he was granted a new trial by the Georgia Court of Appeals.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 51.

Name: Milton Harvey
Body: Fourteen-year-old Milton Harvey went missing after running an errand on his bicycle in September 1979. His tragic death marked one of the earliest heartbreaks in a terrorizing wave of disappearances that gripped Atlanta's Black community, leaving a grieving city demanding answers for its lost children.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Yusef Bell
Body: Nine-year-old Yusef Bell vanished in October 1979 after walking to a neighborhood store to buy Bruton Snuff for a neighbor. His heartbreaking loss galvanized a community in mourning and galvanized local mothers, including his mother Camille Bell, to form the Committee to Stop Children’s Murders and demand a dedicated task force.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Aaron Wyche
Body: A gentle 10-year-old, Aaron Wyche disappeared in June 1980 after being seen near a local grocery store. His death heightened fear across the city as families realized the mysterious killer was targeting boys of varying ages across metropolitan Atlanta.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Aaron Jackson
Body: Nine-year-old Aaron Jackson disappeared in November 1980, another precious life lost during a terrifying season of fear, driving community leaders and federal investigators to intensify their relentless search for justice.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Patrick Rogers
Body: A vibrant 16-year-old with an infectious spirit, Patrick Rogers was a multi-talented teenager and aspiring musician who lifted spirits by writing music with his friend, Joe Harper. Known affectionately to friends as "Pat Man," he was a familiar, bright face who often hung out near the fast-food restaurant on Moreland Avenue by I-20. When he suddenly vanished in November 1980, the heart-wrenching news echoed through the neighborhood, underscoring the tragic and far-reaching impact of the crisis on Atlanta's youth.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: Curtis Walker
Body: Thirteen-year-old Curtis Walker went missing in February 1981 while working odd jobs to help support his family. His death underscored the vulnerability of young boys trying to navigate daily life amidst an unprecedented crisis in their hometown.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: William Barrett
Body: Just 17 years old when he disappeared in May 1981, William Barrett's tragic death came during the final months of the harrowing crisis, right as massive local and federal task forces closed in on solving the mysteries behind the disappearances.
Source: 1. “Composite of the 28 Missing or Murdered Children in the Atlanta Child Murders, circa 1980s.” *Digital Library of Georgia*, Georgia State University Library, https://dlg.usg.edu/record/gsu_ajc_14196.  2. “Atlanta Child Murders Part 18 of 24.” *FBI Vault*, Federal Bureau of Investigation, https://vault.fbi.gov/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders/Atlanta%20Child%20Murders%20Part%2018.

Name: John Glover
Body: Breaking historical ground as the first African American to lead an FBI field office, John Glover took the helm during one of the nation's most high-profile investigations. Heading the FBI's involvement with the Atlanta Missing and Murdered Task Force, he navigated intense public pressure and complex cross-agency cooperation to bring federal resources and strategic oversight to the search for answers.
Source: 1. “Serial Killers, Part 5: Wayne Williams and the Atlanta Child Murders.” *Federal Bureau of Investigation*, 7 Feb. 2014, https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders.

Name: Wayne Williams
Body: An ambitious 23-year-old freelance photographer and music promoter, Wayne Williams became the central figure in the investigation after being spotted near a bridge over the Chattahoochee River. Ultimately convicted in 1982 for the murders of two adult victims, he was identified by law enforcement as the primary suspect in the majority of the child disappearances, bringing a dramatic close to a terrifying period in Atlanta's history when the slayings abruptly stopped following his arrest.
Source: 1. “Serial Killers, Part 5: Wayne Williams and the Atlanta Child Murders.” *Federal Bureau of Investigation*, 7 Feb. 2014, https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-serial-killers-part-5-wayne-williams-and-the-atlanta-child-murders.

Name: Irene Dobbs Jackson
Body: Became the first African American to receive a library card from the main Central Library in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1961.
Source: 1. “Auburn Avenue Research Library.” *Building Memories*, Georgia Institute of Technology, https://leading-edge.iac.gatech.edu/building-memories/auburn-avenue-research-library/.  2. Dankowski, Terra, and Carrie Smith. “By the Numbers: Atlanta.” *American Libraries*, 3 Jan. 2017, https://americanlibrariesmagazine.org/2017/01/03/by-the-numbers-atlanta/.

Name: Bishop Henry McNeal Turner
Body:
Born in South Carolina, Henry McNeal Turner moved to Georgia after the Civil War and dedicated himself to planting African Methodist Episcopal congregations across the state. In his view, the church served as the essential foundation for the first schoolhouses, meeting halls, and political training grounds for newly freed people who were not yet fully protected. Beside fellow freedmen, he organized Black men to exercise their newly gained right to vote while encouraging Black women to recognize their political power even without official suffrage, firmly believing that emancipation without active participation was merely another form of control.

Turner witnessed a brief moment when democracy reflected its promises as formerly enslaved men were elected to office, helped draft a new state constitution, and stood in the Georgia Legislature in 1868 as elected representatives. However, Georgia quickly retreated into fear and white supremacy, rewriting laws, expelling Black legislators, and subjecting community leaders to imprisonment, attacks, violence, and exile. Despite his tireless efforts, the Reconstruction era ultimately failed to secure lasting equality, leaving behind a bittersweet legacy of courage in the face of systemic opposition.
Source: 1. Angell, Stephen Ward. “Henry McNeal Turner (1834–1915).” *New Georgia Encyclopedia*, 3 Sept. 2002, https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/henry-mcneal-turner-1834-1915.

Name: Clara A. Howard
Body: Clara A. Howard (1866–1935) enrolled at the Spelman Baptist Seminary in 1881, graduating at the top of its first graduating class in 1887. After teaching in Atlanta for several years, she answered a call from the Women’s Baptist Foreign Missionary Society and moved to Lukunga in the Congo. Joining her Spelman classmate Nora Gordon, who had arrived two years prior, the pair established a school for local children that quickly grew to 100 students, witnessing tremendous growth and development among the young women they taught. However, Howard contracted a severe case of malaria that nearly claimed her life, forcing her to return to Atlanta alongside her most promising student, Flora Zeto Malekebu, who enrolled at Spelman. Though Nora tragically passed away at age 24, Howard survived and lived to age 69; both women, along with Flora, were eventually laid to rest at South-View Cemetery. Howard’s enduring legacy lived on through the Congolese students who followed her path to America and in the naming of Spelman’s Howard-Harreld Hall in her honor.
Source: 1. Historic South-View Preservation Foundation. *Sisters for Eternity: The Spelman College Legacy at South-View Cemetery*. Flyer, 2018.

Name: Casket Scandal
Body:
When Lucius Lee passed away in 1915, his death left a profound vacancy in Atlanta's African American funeral industry. Over a distinguished forty-year career, Lee had built immense community trust through honest dealings and dependable service. His son, Will Lee, who had long partnered in the firm, stepped up to continue his father's legacy, but tragedy struck again when Will passed away in February 1916. Seeking to maintain stability, the family turned to Samuel F. Ware—a Spanish-American War veteran and nephew of Lucius Lee—to take over management of L. L. Lee & Son. Supported by public endorsements from Will's widow, Bessie, and sister, Addie Jackson, Ware managed to rebuild the enterprise on West Mitchell Street after the destructive Great Fire of May 1917, eventually rebranding as the Atlanta Undertaking Company while continuing to leverage the respected Lee family name.

By late 1922, however, unsettling rumors began circulating regarding missing caskets from South-View Cemetery, pointing directly toward Ware. The rumors turned to grim reality on the night of Friday, December 8, when police apprehended two men in the act of exhuming a casket from a fresh grave. Under interrogation, the men confessed that Ware had hired them to unearth caskets for resale. That same night, authorities intercepted Ware carrying two freshly dug caskets and discovered additional stolen caskets at his establishment, leading to his arrest on $10,000 bail. The true horror unfolded the following Monday when distraught families gathered at South-View as police oversaw grave disinterments, only to discover their loved ones had been removed from their caskets and reburied in plain wooden shipping crates.

In the aftermath, South-View issued a public statement of regret, and undertaker David T. Howard was entrusted with the solemn duty of properly reinterring the desecrated bodies, emphasizing in the Atlanta Independent that sacred places must be protected from such trespasses. Stockholders swiftly replaced Ware and disavowed his actions. Though initially convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison, Ware was granted a new trial by the Georgia Court of Appeals; while condemning his "ghoulish" conduct, the court found that removing a casket while lifting a body was not explicitly covered under Georgia's 1922 criminal code.
Source: 1. Henderson, D. L. *South-View: An African American City of the Dead*. Carrelspin Press, 2018, p. 51.
